Glyco-regex syntax, step by step

glyco-regex-syntax.Rmd

What is a pattern?

A pattern is a short description of the feature you want to find in a glycan. For example, Gal-GlcNAc asks for Gal directly attached to GlcNAc. A regular expression, often shortened to regex, adds symbols that express choices, repetition, and conditions. You do not need prior regex knowledge: this guide introduces those symbols one at a time.

Glyco-regex searches the connected residues of a glycan, rather than letters in its written name. Gal means one galactose residue; it does not match the letters “Gal” within GalNAc. Different ways of writing the same branch arrangement do not turn it into a different structural feature.

The Get Started guide introduces the biological motivation and basic workflow. This guide explains the syntax in more detail, including optional advanced features. The examples use small illustrative glycans so that you can check each answer by eye.

library(glyrex)
glycans <- c(
  lacnac = "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-",
  sialylated = "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-",
  fucosylated = "Gal(b1-4)[Fuc(a1-3)]GlcNAc(b1-",
  both = "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)[Fuc(a1-3)]GlcNAc(b1-",
  glcnac = "GlcNAc(b1-"
)
rex_detect(glycans, "Gal-GlcNAc")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE

The first argument is the collection of glycans; the second is the pattern in quotation marks. TRUE means a match was found, and FALSE means none was found. Each answer corresponds to the input with the same name.

Keep structure notation and pattern notation separate

The inputs above use IUPAC-condensed notation to describe structures. The pattern uses glyco-regex notation to describe a search:

Feature Input structure notation Pattern notation
Gal attached by β1–4 to GlcNAc Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc Galb4-GlcNAc
Fuc branch on the same GlcNAc Gal(b1-4)[Fuc(a1-3)]GlcNAc Galb4-(Fuca3-)GlcNAc
Reducing-end α-GlcNAc GlcNAc(a1- GlcNAca$

The ending (b1- in our inputs records the reducing-end anomer and donor position; it does not add another residue. Do not copy IUPAC linkage parentheses into a pattern: Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc is not a valid search pattern.

Patterns are case-sensitive. Write recognized residue names such as Gal and GlcNAc. Spaces in patterns are ignored, although the examples omit them.

One residue, several choices, or any residue

Start with a residue name, a family, or a choice:

Pattern Meaning
Gal One Gal residue
Hex One residue in the Hex family, including Gal, Glc, and Man
HexNAc One residue in the HexNAc family, including GlcNAc and GalNAc
Sia One Neu5Ac, Neu5Gc, or Kdn residue
. Any one residue
[Gal|Man] Either Gal or Man
[^Fuc] One residue other than Fuc
[^Fuc|Xyl] One residue that is neither Fuc nor Xyl

The vertical bar | means “or.” Square brackets collect the alternatives. Each negated alternative (inside [^...]) must describe one residue, not a multi-residue path. The dot does not mean “any number of residues.”

residues <- c("Gal", "GalNAc", "Man", "Fuc")
data.frame(
  residue = residues,
  gal = rex_detect(residues, "Gal"),
  hex = rex_detect(residues, "Hex"),
  gal_or_man = rex_detect(residues, "[Gal|Man]"),
  not_fuc = rex_detect(residues, "[^Fuc]")
)
#>   residue   gal   hex gal_or_man not_fuc
#> 1     Gal  TRUE  TRUE       TRUE    TRUE
#> 2  GalNAc FALSE FALSE      FALSE    TRUE
#> 3     Man FALSE  TRUE       TRUE    TRUE
#> 4     Fuc FALSE FALSE      FALSE   FALSE

Residue modifications matter. For example, Gal6S asks for sulfated Gal, whereas plain Gal does not match that modified residue:

rex_detect("Gal6S(b1-4)GlcNAc", c("Gal6S", "Gal", "."))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE

Use residue names supported by glyrepr. A slash can also express residue choices, as in Gal/Man; [Gal|Man] makes the alternatives more explicit.

Build a connected path

Read from left to right, towards the reducing end. A dash joins adjacent residues:

  • Gal-GlcNAc: Gal attaches directly to GlcNAc.
  • Sia-Gal-GlcNAc: a three-residue path in that order.
  • Gal-.-GlcNAc: exactly one intervening residue between Gal and GlcNAc.

A path may occur inside a larger glycan. Extra residues and branches are allowed unless you add a condition that excludes them. Finding Gal-GlcNAc therefore does not establish that Gal is terminal or that GlcNAc has no other branches.

Alternatives can describe whole paths too:

rex_detect(
  c("Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc", "Gal(b1-3)GalNAc", "Man(a1-3)Man"),
  "[Gal-GlcNAc|Gal-GalNAc]"
)
#> [1]  TRUE  TRUE FALSE

The choice belongs inside the square brackets. A bare Gal|Man is not supported.

Specify a linkage only as precisely as you need

A linkage suffix belongs to the residue before the dash. In Galb4-GlcNAc, b means beta and 4 is the acceptor position on GlcNAc. The donor position is inferred as 1, or 2 for Neu5Ac, Neu5Gc, Kdn, and Sia. Thus Neu5Aca3-Gal describes an α2–3 linkage.

Pattern Linkage requirement
Gal-GlcNAc No linkage constraint
Galb-GlcNAc Beta anomer; no position constraint
Galb4-GlcNAc β1–4
Galb3/4-GlcNAc Beta, with acceptor position 3 or 4
Gal?4-GlcNAc Either anomer, with donor 1 and acceptor 4
Galb?-GlcNAc Beta, with donor 1 and any acceptor position 
linkages <- c(
  beta4 = "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc",
  beta3 = "Gal(b1-3)GlcNAc",
  alpha4 = "Gal(a1-4)GlcNAc",
  unknown_position = "Gal(b1-?)GlcNAc"
)
rex_detect(linkages, "Galb4-GlcNAc")
#>            beta4            beta3           alpha4 unknown_position 
#>             TRUE            FALSE            FALSE            FALSE
rex_detect(linkages, "Galb3/4-GlcNAc")
#>            beta4            beta3           alpha4 unknown_position 
#>             TRUE             TRUE            FALSE            FALSE

The glycan must be at least as specific as the pattern. Unknown fields in the pattern act as wildcards; unknown input fields cannot satisfy a specified value. The unknown-position example therefore does not match Galb4-GlcNAc. Every possible input position must be allowed by the pattern: input 4 matches pattern 3/4, but input 3/4 does not match pattern 4. Equal sets of possible positions match.

A linkage suffix is checked even on the final residue of a pattern. For example, GlcNAcb3 requires that GlcNAc attach onwards by β1–3, although that next residue is not included in the match. At the reducing end there is no outgoing glycosidic linkage, so an acceptor position cannot match there. Use GlcNAca$, rather than GlcNAca4$, for reducing-end α-GlcNAc.

Restrict where the match occurs

These symbols test position without adding residues to the result:

Pattern Position required
^Gal Gal is at a non-reducing terminus
GlcNAc$ GlcNAc is the reducing-end residue
Gal% Gal is internal: neither terminal nor reducing-end 
rex_detect(glycans, "^Galb4-GlcNAc")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE       FALSE       FALSE
rex_detect(glycans, "Gal%")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>       FALSE        TRUE       FALSE        TRUE       FALSE
rex_detect(glycans, "GlcNAcb$")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE

Only the uncapped Gal residues satisfy ^Gal. In the sialylated examples, Gal is internal and satisfies Gal% instead. The symbol ^ means something different inside a negated choice: [^Fuc] excludes a residue identity; it does not ask for a terminus.

Even ^Gal-GlcNAc$ need not describe the whole glycan: extra branches on GlcNAc remain allowed. The two symbols constrain the ends of the selected path, not the total number of residues in the structure.

Describe branches on a shared residue

Ordinary parentheses mean a branch. In Galb4-(Fuca3-)GlcNAc, Gal and Fuc both attach to GlcNAc:

Gal --β1–4-->
             GlcNAc
Fuc --α1–3-->

Read (Fuca3-) as “also require a Fucα1–3 branch on the following residue.” Keep its attachment dash inside the parentheses and place GlcNAc immediately after the closing parenthesis.

rex_detect(glycans, "Galb4-(Fuca3-)GlcNAc")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>       FALSE       FALSE        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE
rex_extract(glycans["fucosylated"], "Galb4-(Fuca3-)GlcNAc")
#>                      fucosylated 
#> "Fuc(a1-3)[Gal(b1-4)]GlcNAc(b1-"

A required branch is included in the extracted match. A branch can contain a path, such as (Galb4-GlcNAcb6-)Man, and branches can be nested:

nested <- "Gal(b1-4)[Gal(b1-4)[Fuc(a1-3)]GlcNAc(b1-6)]GlcNAc"
rex_detect(nested, "Galb4-(Galb4-(Fuca3-)GlcNAcb6-)GlcNAc")
#> [1] TRUE

Work from the inside out: the inner Fuc attaches to the branch GlcNAc; that GlcNAc attaches by β1–6 to the final GlcNAc. The outer Gal attaches by β1–4 to that final GlcNAc. Extra branches are still allowed.

Require a branch to be absent

Add ! immediately inside the parentheses:

rex_detect(glycans, "Galb4-(!Fuc-)GlcNAc")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE       FALSE       FALSE

This requires the Gal–GlcNAc path with no remaining Fuc branch on its GlcNAc. (!Fuca3-) excludes only a compatible α1–3 Fuc branch; (!Fuc-) excludes Fuc with any linkage. An absence condition can describe a longer branch too, for example Gal-(!Fuc-Man-)GlcNAc.

The word remaining matters: the check examines branches not already used by the preceding pattern. Fuc-(!Fuc-)GlcNAc can match a single Fuc attached to GlcNAc; it asks for no additional Fuc branch there.

Three different meanings of “not”

Question How to express it
Is a non-Fuc residue attached to GlcNAc? [^Fuc]-GlcNAc
Does this GlcNAc lack a Fuc branch? (!Fuc-)GlcNAc
Does the entire glycan lack Fuc? rex_detect(glycans, "Fuc", negate = TRUE) 
data.frame(
  glycan = names(glycans),
  non_fuc_neighbor = unname(rex_detect(glycans, "[^Fuc]-GlcNAc")),
  no_fuc_branch = unname(rex_detect(glycans, "(!Fuc-)GlcNAc")),
  no_fuc_anywhere = unname(rex_detect(glycans, "Fuc", negate = TRUE))
)
#>        glycan non_fuc_neighbor no_fuc_branch no_fuc_anywhere
#> 1      lacnac             TRUE          TRUE            TRUE
#> 2  sialylated             TRUE          TRUE            TRUE
#> 3 fucosylated             TRUE         FALSE           FALSE
#> 4        both             TRUE         FALSE           FALSE
#> 5      glcnac            FALSE          TRUE            TRUE

The fucosylated LacNAc has a non-Fuc neighbour (Gal), so it passes the first column. GlcNAc alone has no neighbour, so it fails that column but passes the absence checks. A local branch condition says nothing about fucose elsewhere in a larger structure.

Optional residues and repeated units

Put the unit in square brackets, then say how many copies are allowed. The symbol or braces after the group apply to the whole group.

Form Number of consecutive copies
[Gal]? Zero or one
[Gal]* Zero or more
[Gal]+ One or more
[Gal]{2} Exactly two
[Gal]{2,4} Two to four
[Gal]{2,} At least two
[Gal]{,4} Zero to four

For example, [Sia]?-Galb4-GlcNAc allows an optional Sia before LacNAc:

rex_detect(glycans, "[Sia]?-Galb4-GlcNAc")
#>      lacnac  sialylated fucosylated        both      glcnac 
#>        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE       FALSE

Optional does not mean forbidden: both sialylated and unsialylated LacNAc can match. Because a match may start within a glycan, even the zero-copy choice can find a capped Gal. Add terminal or neighbouring-path conditions if you need to distinguish those cases.

A repeated group can contain several residues:

repeat_glycan <- "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-3)Gal(b1-"
rex_extract(repeat_glycan, "[Galb4-GlcNAcb3]{2}")
#> [1] "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-"

This repeats the Gal–GlcNAc unit twice. The b3 on GlcNAc constrains its attachment to the next residue, including the final attachment beyond the selected two units. It is a connected path, not a request for two copies anywhere in the glycan. Use rex_count() for counting occurrences.

Use [Gal]+, not Gal+. The alternative grouping syntax (?:Galb4-GlcNAcb3){2} has the same purpose as square brackets; plain parentheses would mean a branch.

A branch can also be optional, as in Galb4-(Fuca3-)?GlcNAc. It allows the Fuc branch to participate in the match but does not exclude other branches or other Fuc linkages when that optional branch is skipped.

Prefer longer or shorter repeats

By default, repetition tries longer runs first. This is called greedy matching. Add ? after the repetition symbol to try shorter runs first, called lazy matching. The rest of the pattern must succeed either way.

chain <- "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-4)GlcNAc"
rex_extract(chain, "Hex-[HexNAc]+")
#> [1] "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-4)GlcNAc(?1-"
rex_extract(chain, "Hex-[HexNAc]+?")
#> [1] "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-"

The first includes both GlcNAc residues; the second includes just one. In [Gal]?, the question mark means optional; in [Gal]+?, it changes which repetition length is tried first. In Gal?4, it instead belongs to the linkage suffix. Use the bracketed form [Gal]? to make optionality clear.

Even when zero copies are allowed, glyrex does not return an empty match: [Gal]* on a glycan without Gal does not produce a successful zero-residue result. Unbounded repetition is limited by the residues in the input glycan.

Check neighbours without including them (advanced)

Sometimes you want to extract Gal only when it has particular neighbours. A lookaround assertion checks a neighbouring path without adding those neighbours to the match. “Ahead” means towards the reducing end; “behind” means towards the non-reducing side.

Pattern Condition; only Gal is included
Gal-(?=GlcNAc) The next residue towards the reducing end is GlcNAc
Gal-(?!GlcNAc) That next residue is not GlcNAc, or there is none
(?<=Sia-)Gal A Sia is directly attached on the non-reducing side
(?<!Sia-)Gal No Sia is directly attached on the non-reducing side 
x <- "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(a1-"
rex_extract(x, "Sia-Gal-GlcNAc")
#> [1] "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(a1-"
rex_extract(x, "(?<=Sia-)Gal-(?=GlcNAc)")
#> [1] "Gal(b1-"
rex_detect(x, "(?<!Sia-)Gal")
#> [1] FALSE

The first extraction includes all three residues; the second returns Gal only. Its output retains the Gal anomer in Gal(b1-. All paths inside assertions are still written towards the reducing end: do not reverse the order of a multi-residue path inside a lookbehind.

Unlike branch absence, negative lookbehind considers even residues already included in the path. On Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc, Gal-(!Gal-)GlcNAc succeeds (no additional Gal branch), but Gal-(?<!Gal-)GlcNAc fails (Gal is attached).

A lookbehind immediately before a branch checks that branch. For example, Gal-(?<!Sia-)(Gal-)GlcNAc requires an additional Gal branch on GlcNAc whose Gal is not capped directly by Sia. It does not test whether GlcNAc itself has Sia attached.

Assertions only check conditions. They cannot be repeated, and a pattern consisting only of an assertion, such as (?=Gal), returns no match because it includes no residues.

Give part of a match a name (advanced)

A named capture labels a selected part so you can retrieve it separately. Write (?<name>...), replacing name with a useful label:

rex_match(
  glycans,
  "(?<cap>Sia)-(?<unit>Galb4-GlcNAc)"
)
#>             match                             cap         
#> lacnac      NA                                NA          
#> sialylated  "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-" "Neu5Ac(a2-"
#> fucosylated NA                                NA          
#> both        "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-" "Neu5Ac(a2-"
#> glcnac      NA                                NA          
#>             unit                 
#> lacnac      NA                   
#> sialylated  "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-"
#> fucosylated NA                   
#> both        "Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-"
#> glcnac      NA

The match column contains the full match; cap and unit contain the labelled parts. Inputs without a match have missing values. Captures include residues in the full match, whereas lookarounds only test their presence. Ordinary branch parentheses do not create a named column.

Names must start with a letter and contain only letters, digits, or underscores. Use each name once, and do not use the reserved name match. Use rex_match_all() to retrieve all retained matches and their captures.

Build and check your own pattern

Start with the required residues, then add one condition at a time:

Step Pattern Added requirement
1 Gal-GlcNAc Adjacent Gal and GlcNAc
2 Galb4-GlcNAc β1–4 linkage
3 Sia-Galb4-GlcNAc Sialic acid on Gal
4 ^Sia-Galb4-GlcNAc That sialic acid is terminal
5 ^Sia-Galb4-(!Fuc-)GlcNAc No remaining Fuc branch on that GlcNAc 
pattern <- rex_compile("^Sia-Galb4-(!Fuc-)GlcNAc")
rex_subset(glycans, pattern)
#>                        sialylated 
#> "Neu5Ac(a2-3)Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc(b1-"

rex_compile() checks the syntax and prepares a reusable pattern. It does not establish that the pattern asks the biological question you intended. Try known positive and negative structures, and inspect extracted matches.

Common mistake Use instead
IUPAC linkage in a pattern: Gal(b1-4)GlcNAc Galb4-GlcNAc
Attachment dash outside branch: Gal-(Fuc)-GlcNAc Gal-(Fuc-)GlcNAc
Ordinary parentheses for a repeated path: (Gal)+ [Gal]+
Bare alternatives: Gal|Man [Gal|Man]
Bare negation: !Fuc or [!Fuc] [^Fuc] for a non-Fuc residue; (!Fuc-) for branch absence
Using . to skip an arbitrary path [.]* for zero or more connected residues

Interpret the results in structural terms

  • rex_detect() asks whether a match exists; rex_subset() keeps matching inputs. Missing inputs give NA in detection, and are omitted by subsetting.
  • rex_extract() returns one retained match; rex_extract_all() returns all retained matches. Extracted strings use standardized IUPAC notation.
  • rex_count() counts retained structural matches, not glycan abundance. glyrex keeps the first successful match per starting residue, then removes matches wholly contained in larger matches. Remaining matches may overlap; it does not enumerate every possible combination of alternatives or branches.
  • Matches are ordered by decreasing residue count, then starting residue ID. The first result is not necessarily the leftmost text in the input string.
  • rex_locate() and rex_locate_all() report graph residue and edge IDs, not character positions in a string.

The input must describe a supported connected structure. Composition alone cannot answer connectivity questions, and floating parts or unspecified branch placement are not supported. Invalid structures produce errors rather than FALSE. Unspecified pattern fields accept unknown input information, but specified constraints require input information at least as specific.

See ?rex_compile for compiling reusable patterns and ?rex_detect for query functions and result conventions.
